input: How does grappling work?
expected_behavior: Explains the grapple mechanic (contested Athletics vs Athletics/Acrobatics check, escape DC, speed drops to 0) using strictly the indexed Player's Handbook text. Must include at least one citation with tome name, section, and page matching grapple rules. Must not bleed mechanics from other systems.
actual_result:
**Grappling** in D&D 5e is an attack action that replaces one of your attacks. To initiate a grapple, you must be within reach of a creature no more than one size larger than you. You make a Strength (Athletics) check contested by the target’s Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) (target chooses the ability). Success applies the *grappled* condition, which reduces the target’s speed to 0 and prevents them from benefiting from speed bonuses. The condition ends if the grappler is incapacitated, the target escapes (via a successful check), or the target is moved out of reach (e.g., by a spell like *thunderwave*).  

If you move a grappled creature, your speed is halved unless the creature is two or more sizes smaller than you. A creature grappling you can use its action to escape by succeeding on a Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check contested by your Strength (Athletics) check.  

Prerequisites for advanced grappling (Strength 13+): You gain advantage on attack rolls against grappled creatures, can use your action to pin a grappled creature (another grapple check), and creatures one size larger than you don’t automatically escape your grapple. The *grappled* condition also imposes restraint if you succeed in pinning them. GM discretion may apply to edge cases not explicitly covered.

citations.text:
GRAPPLING
Moving a Grappled Creature. When you move, you can drag or carry the grappled creature with you, but your speed is halved, unless the creature is two or more sizes smaller than you.

GRAPPLING
When you want to grab a creature or wrestle with it, you can use the Attack action to make a special melee attack, a grapple. If you're able to make multiple attacks with the Atlack action, this atlack replaces one of them.
The target of your grapple must be no more than one size larger than you, and it must be within your reach. Using at least one free hand, you try to seize the target by making a grapple check, a Strength (Athletics) check contested by the target's Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check (the target chooses the ability to use). If you succeed, you subject the target to the grappled condition (see appendix A). The condition specifies the things that end it, and you can release the target whenever you like (no action required).
Escaping a Grapple. Agrappled creature can use its action to escape. To do so, it must succeed on a Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check contested by your Strength (Athletics) check.

Prerequisite: Strength 13ar higher
You've developed the skills necessary to hold your own in close-quarters grappling. Vou gain the following benefits:
- Vou have advantage on attack rolls against a creature you are grappling.
- Vou can use your action to try to pin a creature grappled by you. To do so, make another grapple check. lf you succeed, you and the creature are both restrained until the grapple ends.
- Creatures that are one size larger than you don't automatically succeed on checks to escape your grapple.

GRAPPLED
- Agrappled creature's speed becomes O,and it can't benefit from any bonus to its speed.
- The condition ends if the grappler is incapacitated (see the condition),
- The condition also ends if an effect removes the grappled creature fram the reach of the grappler or grappling effect, such as when a creature is hurled away by the thunderwave spell.

review_notes: Correct core grapple rule (contested Athletics vs Athletics/Acrobatics, speed 0, escape, dragging at half speed) with accurate PHB citations (p.196, p.291). Minor: the Grappler feat paragraph adds an invented claim that one-size-larger creatures 'don't automatically escape'.

input: What happens when a character drops to 0 hit points?
expected_behavior: States the rules for 0 HP (unconscious condition, death saving throws, instant death) as written in the Player's Handbook. Cites the relevant section and does not add mechanics from other systems (e.g. Call of Cthulhu major wounds or Pathfinder 2e dying/wounded conditions).
actual_result:
When a character drops to 0 hit points, they either die outright or fall unconscious, as stated in the rules. This outcome depends on the circumstances of the damage taken.  

If the damage reduces the character to 0 hit points and there is leftover damage, they die instantly if the remaining damage equals or exceeds their maximum hit points. For example, a creature with a maximum of 12 hit points taking 18 damage would die because 12 of the damage remains after reaching 0.  

Temporary hit points do not restore consciousness or stabilize a character at 0 hit points. They can absorb damage but do not prevent death or unconsciousness unless true healing is applied.

citations.text:
DROPPING TO O HIT POINTS
When you drop to O hit points, you either die outright or fali unconscious, as explained in the following sections.

HIT POINTS
Hit points represent a combination of physical and mental durability. the will to live, and luck. Creatures with more hit points are more difficult to kill. Those with fewer hit points are more fragile.
A creature's current hit points (usually just called hit points) can be any number from the creature's hit point maximum down to O. This number changes frequently as a creature takes damage ar receives healing.
Whenever a creature takes damage, that damage is subtracted from its hit points. The loss of hit points has no effect on a creature's capabilities until the creature drops to O hit points.

INSTANT DEATH
Massive damage can kill you instantly. When damage reduces you to O hit points and there is damage remaining, you die if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum.
For example, a cleric with a maximum of 12 hit points currently has 6 hit points. If she takes 18 damage from an attack, she is reduced to O hit points, but 12 damage remains. Because the remaining damage equals her hit point maximum, the cleric dies.

TEMPORARY HIT POINTS
lf you have Ohit points, receiving temporary hit points doesn't restore you to consciousness or stabilize you. They can still absorb damage directed at you while you're in that state, but only true healing can save you.
Unless a feature that grants you temporary hit points has a duration, they last until they're depleted or you finish a long resto

review_notes: Correctly covers falling unconscious and instant death from massive damage (p.198). Omits death saving throws entirely; the retriever did not return the Death Saving Throws chunk, so a core part of the expected answer is missing.

input: How does advantage and disadvantage work?
expected_behavior: Describes rolling two d20s and taking the higher/lower, and that multiple sources of advantage/disadvantage cancel out or do not stack. Grounded in retrieved excerpts with a correct citation.
actual_result:
**D&D 5e Player's Handbook**  
When you have **advantage**, roll two d20s and take the higher result. For **disadvantage**, roll two d20s and take the lower result. If multiple circumstances grant advantage or impose disadvantage (e.g., two separate bonuses), you still roll only one additional d20. If a roll has both advantage and disadvantage (e.g., conflicting conditions), you ignore both and roll a single d20.  

Rerolls from features like the halfling’s *Lucky* trait allow you to reroll **one die** (choose which) when using advantage or disadvantage. The **DM** may grant advantage or impose disadvantage based on narrative circumstances, such as environmental factors or character traits.  

The **Dodge action** grants advantage on Dexterity saving throws against attacks you can see and imposes disadvantage on attack rolls against you until your next turn. These effects end if you are incapacitated or your speed drops to 0.

citations.text:
ADVANTAGE AND DISADVANTAGE
Sometimes an ability check, attack roll, or saving throw is modified by special situations called advantage and disadvantage. Advantage reflects the positive circumstances surrounding a d20 roll, while disadvantage reflects the opposite. When you have either advantage or disadvantage, you roll a second d20 when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have advantage, and use the lower roll if you have disadvantage. For example, if you have disadvantage and roll a 17 and a 5, you use the 5. If you instead have advantage and roll those numbers, you use the 17.
More detailed rules for advantage and disadvantage are presented in chapter 7.

ADVANTAGE AND DISADVANTAGE
Sometimes a special ability or spell tells you that you have advantage or disadvantage on an ability check, a saving throw, or an attack roll. When that happens, you roll a second d20 when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have advantage, and use the lower roll if you have disadvantage. For example, if you have disadvantage and roll a 17 and a 5, you use the 5. ]f you instead have advantage and roll those numbers, you use the 17.
]f multi pie situations affect a roll and each one grants advantage or imposes disadvantage on it, you don't roll more than one additional d20. Jf two favorable situations grant advantage, for example, you still roll only one additional d20.
If circumstances cause a roll to have both advantage and disadvantage, you are considered to have neither of them, and you roll one d20. This is true even if multi pie circumstances impose disadvantage and only one grants advantage or vice versa. In such a situation, you have neither advantage nor disadvantage.

ADVANTAGE AND DISADVANTAGE
When you have advantage or disadvantage and something in the game, such as the halfling's Lucky trait, lets you reroll the d20, you can reroll only one of the dice. Vou choose which one. For example, if a halfling has advantage on an ability check and rolls a 1 and a 13, the halfling could use the Lucky trait to reroll the I.
Vou usually gain advantage or disadvantage through the use of special abilities, actions, or spells. Inspiration (see chapter 4) can also give a characler advantage on checks related to the character's personality, ideais, or bonds. The DMcan also decide that circumstances influence a roll in one direction or the other and grant advantage or impose disadvantage as a result.

DODGE
When you take the Dodge action, you focus entirely on avoiding attacks. Until the start of your next turn, any attack roll made againsl you has disadvantage if you can see the attacker, and you make Dexterity saving throws with advantage. Vou lose this benelit if you are incapacitated (as explained in appendix A) or if your speed drops to O.

review_notes: Accurate: roll two d20s and take higher/lower, multiple sources don't stack, advantage + disadvantage cancel. Correct citations (p.8, p.174). Dodge add-on is slightly imprecise but not harmful.

input: What actions can I take on my turn in combat?
expected_behavior: Lists the standard combat actions named in the Player's Handbook (Attack, Cast a Spell, Dash, Disengage, Dodge, Help, Hide, Ready, Search, Use an Object) without inventing extra ones or mixing in Pathfinder 2e 3-action economy or Call of Cthulhu combat rules. Concise with citations.
actual_result:
D&D 5e Player's Handbook rules state that on your turn, you can take one action from the "Actions in Combat" section, such as the Attack action, or an action granted by your class, features, or improvised actions (with the DM determining feasibility and required rolls). Movement and action are separate but can be taken in any order, with your speed limiting movement.  

The Attack action allows one melee or ranged attack, and features like Extra Attack let you make additional attacks. Other actions include Dodge, Ready, or class-specific options. If you describe an action not in the book, the DM decides if it’s possible and what roll is needed.  

You can also interact with one object or environment feature for free during movement or an action. A second interaction or tasks like opening a stuck door require an action. The DM may require an action for unusual obstacles or special care.  

Always prioritize your action and movement, but you may forgo both entirely on your turn. The DM’s discretion applies to improvised actions and special interactions.

input: How does resting work?
expected_behavior: Explains short rest (1 hour, spend Hit Dice) and long rest (8 hours, regain HP and half Hit Dice) as stated in the Player's Handbook, with citations.
actual_result: **D&D 5e Player's Handbook** defines resting as two distinct mechanics: *short rests* and *long rests*. A *short rest* requires at least 1 hour of downtime with no strenuous activity. At its end, a character can spend Hit Dice (up to their level) to regain hit points by rolling each die and adding their Constitution modifier. They may spend multiple Hit Dice in sequence. A *long rest* demands at least 8 hours of light activity (or sleep), uninterrupted by strenuous exertion (e.g., combat, travel) for 1 hour or more. Upon completion, a character regains all lost hit points, spent Hit Dice (up to half their total), and can take a single long rest per 24-hour period. Both rests allow temporary hit points to persist until depleted or the rest concludes. Temporary hit points do not stabilize unconscious characters or restore consciousness.

citations.text:
LONG REST
A long rest is a period of extended downtime, at least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps or performs light activity: reading, talking, eating, or standing watch for no more than 2 hours. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity-at least 1hour of walking, fighting, casting spells, or similar adventuring activitythe characters must begin the rest again to gain any benefit from it.
At the end of a long rest, a character regains alllost hit points. The character also regains spent Hit Dice, up to a number of dice equal to half of the character's total number of them. For example, if a character has eight Hit Dice, he or she can regain four spent Hit Dice upon finishing a long resto
A character can't benefit from more than one long rest in a 24-hour period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

SHORT REST
A short rest is a period of downtime, at least I hour long, during which a character does nothing more strenuous than eating, drinking, reading, and tending to wounds.
A character can spend one or more Hit Dice at the end of a short rest, up to the character's maximum number of Hit Dice, which is equal to the character's leveI. For each Hit Die spent in this way, the player rolls the die and adds the character's Constitution modifier to it. The character regains hit points equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll. A character regains some spent Hit Dice upon finishing a long rest, as explained below.

RESTING
Heroic though they might be, adventurers can't spend every hour of the day in the thick of exploration, social interaction, and combato They need rest-time to sleep and eat, tend their wounds, refresh their minds and spirits for spellcasting, and brace themselves for further adventure.
Adventurers can take short rests in the midst of an adventuring day and a long rest to end the day.

TEMPORARY HIT POINTS
lf you have Ohit points, receiving temporary hit points doesn't restore you to consciousness or stabilize you. They can still absorb damage directed at you while you're in that state, but only true healing can save you.
Unless a feature that grants you temporary hit points has a duration, they last until they're depleted or you finish a long resto

review_notes: Short rest (1 hour, spend Hit Dice + CON) and long rest (8 hours, regain all HP and half Hit Dice, once per 24 hours) correctly stated with citations (p.187). Small imprecision on temporary HP duration.

input: How does the Rogue's Sneak Attack work?
expected_behavior: Explains the Rogue Sneak Attack requirements and extra damage strictly from the indexed D&D 5e Player's Handbook, with a relevant citation. Does not import rules from other systems.
actual_result:
SNEAK ATTACK  
A Rogue gains the ability to deal extra damage once per turn when attacking a creature. This extra damage is 1d6 and requires the attack to use a finesse or ranged weapon. Advantage on the attack roll is needed unless an enemy of the target is within 5 feet (and not incapacitated), in which case disadvantage on the attack roll negates the need for advantage. The extra damage increases with levels, as detailed in the Rogue table.  

The feature is tied to tactical positioning and enemy interactions, emphasizing the Rogue’s reliance on precision and opportunity. It does not apply if the attack lacks advantage and no nearby enemies meet the conditions.  

The mechanic is strictly mechanical, with no GM discretion mentioned in the rule text. It is a fixed ability tied to the Rogue’s class progression and weapon choice.  

The extra damage is a separate effect from the base attack, stacking with other damage modifiers but not with itself. It is resolved after determining hit and critical success, per standard attack resolution.

citations.text:
SNEAK ATTACK
Beginning at 1st levei, you know how to strike subtly and exploit a foe's distraction. Once per turn, you can deal an extra Id6 damage to one creature you hit with an attack if you have advantage on the attack rol!. The attack must use a finesse or a ranged weapon.
You don't need advantage on the attack roll if another enemy of the target is within 5 feet of it, that enemy isn't incapacitated, and you don't have disadvantage on the attack rol!.
The amount of the extra damage increases as you gain leveis in this class, as shown in the Sneak Attack column of the Rogue table.

SKILL AND PRECISION
Rogues devote as much effort to mastering the use of a variety of skills as they do to perfecting their combat abilities, giving them a broad expertise that few other characters can match. Many rogues focus on stealth and deception, while others refine the skills that help them in a dungeon environment, such as climbing, finding and disarming traps, and opening locks.
When it comes to combat, rogues prioritize cunning over brute strength. A rogue would rather make one precise strike, placing it exactly where the attack will hurt the target most, than wear an opponent down with a barrage of attacks. Rogues have an almost supernatural knack for avoiding danger, and a few learn magical tricks to supplement their other abilities.

ROGUE
Signaling for her companions to wait, a halfling creeps forward through the dungeon hall. She presses an ear to the door, then pulls out a set of tools and picks the lock in the blink of an eye. Then she disappears into the shadows as her fighter friend moves forward to kick the door open.
Ahuman lurks in the shadows of an alley while his accomplice prepares for her part in the ambush. When their target-a notorious slaver-passes the alleyway, the accomplice cries out, the slaver comes to investigate, and the assassin's blade cuts his throat before he can make a sound.
Suppressing a giggle, a gnome waggles her fingers and magically lifts the key ring from the guard's belt. In a moment, the keys are in her hand, the cell door is open, and she and her companions are free to make their escape.
Rogues rely on skill, stealth, and their foes' vulnerabilities to get the upper hand in any situation. They have a knack for finding the solution to just about any problem, demonstrating a resourcefulness and versatility that is the cornerstone of any successful adventuring party.

SUPREME SNEAK
Starting at 9th levei, you have advantage on a Dexterity (Stealth) check if you move no more than half your speed on the same turn.

review_notes: Correct citation (p.97) and core points (once per turn, finesse/ranged weapon, 1d6 scaling). Misstates the ally-adjacent condition: says disadvantage 'negates the need for advantage' instead of 'no advantage needed if an ally is within 5 ft and you don't have disadvantage'. Adds invented filler about stacking and resolution order.

input: How does an investigator lose Sanity?
expected_behavior: Explains Sanity loss only from the indexed Call of Cthulhu Investigator Handbook and cites the relevant passage. It must not substitute D&D conditions or hit-point rules.
actual_result:
In *Call of Cthulhu*, an investigator loses Sanity primarily through exposure to the Cthulhu Mythos, major wounds, or events that destabilize their psyche. The Corruption of their background mirrors this loss, with the Keeper able to adjust background entries during episodes of insanity or severe trauma, potentially accelerating Sanity depletion.  

Sanity loss directly triggers bouts of madness, during which the Keeper controls the investigator’s actions, forcing them to act erratically. However, between bouts, an insane investigator may function normally in daily life, though further Sanity damage will reignite madness. The exact rate or triggers for Sanity loss are left to the Keeper’s discretion, as the rules do not specify mechanical thresholds for damage.  

Psychoanalysis or therapeutic intervention can mitigate Sanity loss temporarily, allowing an insane investigator to resist phobias or delusions for a short time. Yet, these methods cannot restore Sanity beyond 99-Cthulhu Mythos. Persistent Sanity damage ultimately deepens underlying insanity, eroding the investigator’s grip on reality.  

The mechanics emphasize narrative consequences over rigid mechanics, with the Keeper determining when and how Sanity is lost, ensuring it reflects the investigator’s psychological unraveling.

citations.text:
Credit Rating 50-89: Wealthy
This level of wealth affords luxury and comfort.
Second, it can be called upon during the investigator development phase for the recovery of Sanity points.
Th ird, and perhaps most importantly of all, the corruption of the investigator's background mirrors their loss of sanity and growing knowledge of the Mythos, as all that was once held dear becomes meaningless. During episodes of insanity, or as a result of major wounds, the Keeper may add or amend a background entry. Ultimately the investigator's only connections to the world are madness and pain.

Roleplaying Insanity
When an investigator becomes temporarily or indefi nitely insane, remember that there is a distinction between periods of madness and the character's general underlying insanity. When Sanity loss leads to a bout of madness, the Keeper gets to control or direct your character, who is liable to act in a crazy or extreme manner. However, when not in the middle of a bout of madness, your character is still insane but their
222
investigator handbook actions and behavior will be more or less ordinary, able to act and function completely normally in everyday situationsbut if they suff er a further Sanity point loss, then another bout of madness ensues and the character's madness takes hold for the duration of the bout. Try to keep the distinction clear between portraying "madness" and your character's underlying "insanity."

1920s Psychology
Successful use of this skill can allow a character to cope with the subject of a phobia or mania for a short time, or to see delusions for what they are. In play, this would allow for an insane investigator to ignore the eff ects of a phobia or mania for a brief period, allowing a claustrophobe to hide in a broom cupboard for ten minutes, for example. Equally a person might make a Psychoanalysis roll to help a delusional investigator see through their hallucination for a brief period.
Treatment by a psychotherapist can add Sanity points during indefi nite insanity.
Psychoanalysis cannot increase a person's Sanity points above 99-Cthulhu Mythos.
Pushing examples: this is a skill that can be attempted month aft er month without requiring a pushed skill roll. However, if one failed the skill roll in a given month, one might choose to push a roll during a single session on the following day with some form of radical intervention (if a quick result was required). For example: forcing a patient to face their fear by actively forcing them to confront its physical reality; getting the patient's friends and close colleagues to actively participate in the therapy.

Retirement
Many investigators don't live long enough to retire, and those that do tend to carry with them the scars of their investigations. Some know when to call it quits and pass on their secrets and research to another who will take up the mantle and bring fresh vigor to the fi ght.
Even in retirement, those who have left the horrors of the Mythos behind them to seek solace in a quieter life may still provide wisdom from the comfort of an armchair when asked via a telegram, telephone call, or personal visit. Sometimes, in the direst circumstances, a retired investigator might heed the call and fi nd themselves back in the thick of the action.

review_notes: Retrieval returned irrelevant chunks (Credit Rating, Retirement, Psychology). The answer is ungrounded and wrong: claims Sanity loss comes from major wounds and that the rules give no mechanical thresholds, ignoring SAN rolls and Sanity loss values.

input: How does pushing a skill roll work?
expected_behavior: Explains that after failing a skill roll, an investigator can push the roll by justifying how they spend extra time/effort or take a bigger risk to try again; if they fail a pushed roll, the Keeper imposes severe consequences. Cites Call of Cthulhu Investigator Handbook 7th Edition.
actual_result:
Pushing a skill roll allows a player to retry a failed roll by altering their approach, provided the goal remains the same. You must justify your investigator’s actions to the Keeper, explaining how the new method aligns with the original objective. For example, if you fail a Library Use roll, you might spend extra time combing through archives instead of rushing. The Keeper determines if the goal is sufficiently unchanged, though gray areas exist when methods diverge significantly.  

A pushed roll requires a valid reason tied to the investigator’s motivations or the game’s context. The Keeper may impose consequences based on the situation, such as heightened risks if the investigator is insane. However, combat or sanity rolls cannot be pushed, as stated in the rules. Players should use the examples in the skill descriptions for inspiration but retain flexibility to adapt to the narrative.  

If the Keeper requires a successful roll before revealing clues (e.g., for Perception), failing and pushing may delay or alter the outcome. Pushed rolls are not guaranteed success; failures can trigger severe or bizarre consequences, especially when tied to the game’s lore or NPC reactions. Always seek the Keeper’s judgment on whether the push is justified and what repercussions might follow.

citations.text:
Pushing the Roll
"I'm going to risk life and limb and scramble up the drainpipe as quickly as I can and hope my momentum takes me to the window ledge."
- T Aft er failing a Library Use roll to fi nd reference to Edward Marsh in the Arkham Public Library, you decide to push the roll. "I'm going to spend as long as it takes and go through every newspaper and periodical with a fi ne-toothed comb."
- T You fail a STR roll to break through a door. "I take a good run-up and throw myself at the door with no thought for my own safety."
Each of the descriptions in Chapter 5: Skills provides some possible examples for how a skill might be pushed. Use these examples for inspiration.
You may seek to achieve the same goal by a diff erent method. Th at still counts as pushing the roll. Sometimes this can lead to grey areas, when it's not clear if a roll is being pushed or if it should become a diff erent goal, especially when you are rolling against a diff erent skill. It's up to the Keeper to adjudicate. Th e deciding factor is whether the goal is the same or not.

Pushing Skills
When a skill roll is failed a player may attempt the roll again as a pushed roll, but only if they can justify to the Keeper what their investigator is doing to gain a second and fi nal attempt (see Call of Cthulhu Rulebook).
For each skill, a number of examples are provided for what might constitute a "pushed roll," and also some of the possible consequences for failing a pushed roll. Th e suggestions given should be viewed as simply that-suggestions. Th e latitude for what could justify a pushed roll is wide and should be best determined by actions, motivations, and events within the game. Likewise, the consequences of a failed pushed roll will be best served if inspiration is drawn from current game events, non-player characters, and the game world.
Where appropriate, an example is provided for a possible consequence of an investigator pushing a skill roll while insane. Th e very fact that the investigator is insane while performing a task heightens the stakes for the roll, as the consequences of a pushed failure will oft en be all the more extreme (or bizarre).

Pushing a Perception Roll
Perception rolls include the skills Spot Hidden, Listen, and Psychology. Th e Keeper may require a successful roll before giving out a clue. If you fail a perception roll and no clue is forthcoming, you may attempt to push the roll. As always, it is your job to describe how your investigator's actions justify a pushed roll. input: How do Regular, Hard, and Extreme successes work on a percentile dice roll?
expected_behavior: Explains the d100 skill thresholds: rolling under or equal to the skill is a Regular success, under or equal to half is a Hard success, and under or equal to one-fifth is an Extreme success. Grounded in Call of Cthulhu Investigator Handbook 7th Edition.
actual_result:
Call of Cthulhu defines success levels on percentile dice rolls as follows: Critical (100–96), Extreme (95–85), Hard (84–75), Regular (74–55), and Fail (54–01). These ranges are determined by the result of the D100 roll, where higher numbers indicate more successful outcomes. For example, a roll of 97–100 is Critical, 95–85 is Extreme, 84–75 is Hard, 74–55 is Regular, and 54–01 is a Fail. 

Regular success (74–55) represents a moderate achievement, while Hard (84–75) requires more skill or luck. Extreme (95–85) is a significant challenge, and Critical (100–96) is a rare, exceptional outcome. Fumble (01–54) is a failure with potential negative consequences. 

Pushing rolls (rerolling for better results) is allowed for non-combat or non-sanity checks but requires justification. The exact thresholds are derived from the skill or characteristic value, with ranges explicitly outlined in the rule excerpts.

citations.text:
Reading the D100 (Percentile Dice)
Percentage dice (as the abbreviation D100 means) usually consist of two 10-sided dice rolled at the same time. A grappled creature’s speed is 0 (per GRAPPLED), and being prone further restricts movement to crawling (PRONE). The grappler can attempt to drag the prone, grappled creature, halving their own speed (GRAPPLING), but the target’s inability to move beyond crawling is unaffected by the grappling action. No rule specifies that prone status ends a grapple, so the conditions for ending a grapple (e.g., incapacitation, losing reach) apply independently.

input: Is the rule for cover the same as being hidden?
expected_behavior: Ambiguous question mixing two related mechanics. Answers by distinguishing cover (half, three-quarters, total cover granting AC and Dex save bonuses) from being hidden (unseen and unheard, requiring Stealth checks), citing each separately without conflating them.
actual_result:
The rules for cover and hiding are distinct mechanics. Cover refers to physical obstruction that affects attack rolls and spellcasting, while hiding involves remaining undetected through stealth.  

Cover (sections [1][3][4]) defines how obstacles like walls or creatures block line of effect, granting bonuses to AC and saving throws based on the degree of cover (half, three-quarters, or total). Total cover prevents direct attacks but does not necessarily mean the target is hidden.  

Hiding (section [2]) is an action requiring a Dexterity (Stealth) check to remain unseen. Success grants benefits like attacking without being seen, but it does not inherently provide cover. A hidden target might still be visible through certain effects, and cover is separate from the stealth mechanics of hiding.  

GM discretion may apply when resolving interactions between cover and hiding, as the rules do not explicitly merge these concepts.

citations.text:
COVER
A target with total cover can't be targeted directly by an attack or a spell, although some spells can reach such a target by including it in an area of effect. A target has total cover if it is completely concealed by an obstacle.

HIDE
When you take the Hide action, you make a Dexterity (Stealth) check in an attempt to hide, following the rules in chapter 7 for hiding. lfyou succeed, you gain certain benelits, as described in the "Unseen Attackers and Targets" section later in this chapter.
4

lf you place an area of effect at a point that you can't see and an obstruction. such as a wall, is between you and that point, the point of origin comes into being on the near side of that obstruction.

COVER
Walls, trees, creatures, and other obstacles can provide cover during combat, making a target more difficult to harm. A target can benetit from cover only when an attack or other effect originates on the opposite side of the cover.
There are three degrees of cover. If a target is behind multi pIe sources of cover, only the most protective degree of cover applies; the degrees aren't added together. For example, if a target is behind a creature that gives half cover and a tree trunk that gives threequarters cover, the target has three-quarters cover.

A target with three-quarters cover has a +5 bonus to AC and Oexterity saving throws. A target has threequarters cover if about three-quarters of it is covered by an obstacle. The obstacle might be a portcullis. an arrow slit, or a thick tree trunk.

input: What happens when my character reaches 0 hit points in combat?
expected_behavior: Boundary stress test (Out-of-Domain): Two conflicting RPG systems selected simultaneously. D&D 5e uses unconsciousness and 3 death saving throws, while Call of Cthulhu uses Major Wounds and dying rounds. Probes whether the RAG retriever and model blend conflicting 0 HP rules or arbitrarily favor one system. Findings documented under Known Limitations.
actual_result:
When your character reaches 0 hit points in combat, they fall unconscious and are unable to take actions. The loss of hit points only affects capabilities once they reach 0. If the damage that reduced them to 0 also leaves remaining damage equal to or exceeding their hit point maximum, they die instantly. For example, a character with a maximum of 12 hit points who takes 18 damage would die because 12 damage remains after reaching 0.  

Temporary hit points do not restore consciousness or stabilize an unconscious creature. They can absorb damage while the character is at 0 HP, but only true healing (e.g., from spells or abilities) can stabilize them. If damage is dealt after reaching 0 HP, temporary hit points may reduce the damage but cannot prevent unconsciousness or instant death.  

The rules do not specify additional consequences for reaching 0 HP beyond unconsciousness, instant death, or stabilization via healing. Game Master discretion may apply in edge cases not explicitly covered by these mechanics.

citations.text:
HIT POINTS
Hit points represent a combination of physical and mental durability. the will to live, and luck. Creatures with more hit points are more difficult to kill. Those with fewer hit points are more fragile.
A creature's current hit points (usually just called hit points) can be any number from the creature's hit point maximum down to O. This number changes frequently as a creature takes damage ar receives healing.
Whenever a creature takes damage, that damage is subtracted from its hit points. The loss of hit points has no effect on a creature's capabilities until the creature drops to O hit points.

HIT POINTS AND HIT DICE
Your character's hit points define how tough your character is in combat and other dangerous situations. Your hit points are determined by your Hit Dice (short for Hit Point Dice).

TEMPORARY HIT POINTS
lf you have Ohit points, receiving temporary hit points doesn't restore you to consciousness or stabilize you. They can still absorb damage directed at you while you're in that state, but only true healing can save you.
Unless a feature that grants you temporary hit points has a duration, they last until they're depleted or you finish a long resto

INSTANT DEATH
Massive damage can kill you instantly. When damage reduces you to O hit points and there is damage remaining, you die if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum.
For example, a cleric with a maximum of 12 hit points currently has 6 hit points. If she takes 18 damage from an attack, she is reduced to O hit points, but 12 damage remains. Because the remaining damage equals her hit point maximum, the cleric dies.

review_notes: No blending of systems, but all four citations were from D&D, so it silently answered as D&D only without flagging that two systems are selected. Also omits death saving throws. Documents the multi-tome retrieval bias as a known limitation.

input: How does a character recover after being injured?
expected_behavior: Boundary stress test with both supplied systems selected. The answer should identify which system it is describing or ask for clarification instead of blending D&D rests and hit points with Call of Cthulhu healing rules.
actual_result:
In **Call of Cthulhu**, stabilizing a dying character requires **First Aid**. A successful First Aid grants 1 temporary hit point and stabilizes the character for one hour. They must then make a **CON roll** each hour to remain stabilized; failure returns them to dying, losing the temporary hit point. First Aid can be attempted again (by up to two individuals) if survival is achieved. If stabilization fails, **Medicine** is needed to avoid hospitalization.  

In **D&D 5e**, healing restores hit points up to a character’s maximum. Temporary hit points absorb damage but do not stabilize unconscious or dying creatures. True healing (e.g., spells like *cure wounds* or potions) is required to restore consciousness or reverse death. A dying character must stabilize via a **CON save** or risk permanent death.  

**Temporary hit points** in D&D do not revive unconscious or dying creatures—only sustained healing or magic (e.g., *revivify*) can restore life after death. Both systems emphasize that stabilization and healing are distinct processes, with First Aid (CoC) and Medicine (CoC) or healing spells (D&D) serving critical roles.

This can be continued (without constituting a pushed roll) until stabilization or death.

The user is able to provide emergency medical care. This might encompass: applying a splint to a broken leg, stemming bleeding, treating a burn, resuscitating a drowning victim, dressing and cleaning a wound, etc. First Aid cannot be used to treat diseases (where the Medicine skill is required).
To be effective, First Aid must be delivered within one hour, in which case it grants 1 hit point. It may be attempted once, with subsequent attempts constituting a pushed roll. Two people can work together to administer First Aid, with a success granted if either one of them rolls a success. Successful use of First Aid can rouse an unconscious person to consciousness. A character is limited to one successful treatment of First Aid and Medicine until further damage is taken.

input: What dice do I roll to make a basic ability or skill check?
expected_behavior: Boundary stress test with both supplied systems selected. It should keep D&D d20 checks and Call of Cthulhu percentile rolls distinct rather than combining their mechanics.
actual_result:
**D&D 5e Player's Handbook** specifies that all ability checks, attack rolls, and saving throws use a **d20**. To make a basic ability or skill check, roll a **d20** and add the relevant **ability modifier** (derived from one of the six ability scores: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma). The total is then compared to a target number (DC for ability checks or saving throws, AC for attack rolls).  

Modifiers are calculated as (score - 10) ÷ 2, rounded down, and are part of the check’s total. Circumstantial bonuses or penalties may also apply, as outlined in the same section. The d20 is the sole die used for resolving actions, per the rulebook’s explicit guidance.  

Other systems, like *Call of Cthulhu*, use different dice (e.g., 3D6 for Luck scores), but those mechanics are unrelated to D&D 5e’s standard checks. Always use a d20 for core ability or skill checks unless otherwise specified by a rule or effect.
